papers.title: Diversified-Risk-Perception Risk Measures and Portfolio Selection
papers.summary: Traditional risk measures generally rely on a single probability model, potentially overlooking information from alternative models and leading to biased risk assessments. This limitation cannot be addressed by asset diversification alone in risk management. In this paper, we propose a Diversified-Risk-Perception (DRP) risk measure framework that integrates asset diversification and risk model diversification to provide a more comprehensive assessment of market risk while reducing reliance on any single model. First, we introduce a flexible exponential aggregation function to evaluate the risk of a portfolio, which accounts for the contributions of all loss components while placing greater emphasis on large losses. Second, we incorporate multiple risk models in the risk measure and optimize their weights based on their perceptions on the risk assessments. As a specific example, we introduce DRP expected shortfall (DRP-ES), establish its theoretical properties, and derive bounds quantifying its sensitivity to model parameters. Empirical experiments in the U.S., Chinese A-share, and South Korean stock markets show that trading strategies based on the DRP-ES achieve higher Sharpe ratios and lower maximum drawdowns than market benchmarks across different periods. Compared with asset diversification strategies based on individual probability models, the DRP strategy exhibits more stable and robust performance across different markets and periods. These findings suggest that the DRP framework can adapt to changing market conditions and improve the stability and effectiveness of portfolio risk management.

papers.title: JUBILEE: A Benchmark Environment for Off-Policy Evaluation in Debt Collections
papers.summary: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the value a candidate decision policy would achieve, using only data logged by the policy already in production. In debt collections, unrecorded factors can influence both actions and outcomes. This paper presents JUBILEE, a benchmark environment built around a debt-collections simulator that generates million-loan panels with competing risks, rare recovery events, and hidden factors driving both outcomes and assignment. The evaluation includes an 80-run comparison of tabular and gradient-boosted estimators under two synthetic outcome mechanisms and a 190-run parameter grid. Independent policy simulations provide reference values with estimated Monte Carlo uncertainty for a synthetic reward score and for simulated cash. With hidden factors influencing action assignment, several tabular methods agree closely while underestimating the field-visit policy's score, an error that also appears with boosted models. Intervals from tabular doubly robust estimation usually contain the reference without hidden assignment dependence but mostly miss it when that dependence is present. Estimates from randomized decisions do not show the same large error, although their limited precision leaves policy choice uncertain. The decision consequences depend on how policy value is defined. The field-visit policy ranks last under the score and first under simulated cash, which excludes channel costs. Under cash, log-based estimators miss this best candidate in nearly every run with hidden assignment dependence in the paired study. JUBILEE supports reproducible study of these failure modes under specified collections mechanisms.
papers.comment: 28 pages, 3 figures, 35 tables. Code: https://github.com/alpha-synthesis/jubilee. Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24008544

papers.title: Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning for an Options Market Maker: An Empirical Study with Real S&P 500 Options
papers.summary: Options market makers absorb client order flow and must hedge the resulting inventory risk under trading frictions. We study whether an option hedging reinforcement learning (RL) agent trained on historical market data outperforms three alternatives in tail-risk protection: (i) traditional delta hedging, (ii) simple hedge-ratio rules, and (iii) the same agent trained in simulated markets. Most RL hedging agents are trained in model-generated markets that do not capture the crashes and volatility regimes present in real data. We introduce an empirical replay environment using S&P 500 option data from 1996 to 2017 and compare against a matched geometric Brownian motion (GBM) environment, a stochastic-volatility (SABR) simulator, and a hybrid that values historical paths with Black-Scholes, all sharing the same portfolio mechanics, stochastic arrivals, costs, and test period. We train a distributional Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) agent and evaluate it out of sample over 2018-2023. The agent trained on empirical data reduces Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) tail loss by 3.1% compared to delta hedging and outperforms every hedge-ratio rule chosen during the training period and every alternative training environment. The reduction reaches 8.9% in volatile and falling markets, but reverses to a cost of 7-10% in rising markets. Empirical training induces a state-dependent short net delta: the policy under-hedges negative-delta books, most strongly after prices have fallen. This tilt disappears with GBM training and is weaker with SABR or hybrid training. These findings suggest that exposure to historical market dynamics can materially change a tail-risk hedging policy, although the evidence rests on a single test path and the edge is regime-conditional.
papers.comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Authors listed alphabetically by last name

papers.title: Worst-Case Contagion in Financial Networks: MILP Clearing and Robust Loss Analysis
papers.summary: We study worst-case contagion losses in financial networks with interbank liabilities and common exposures to marketable assets. Existing linear-programming approaches provide exact stress-test values only within an insolvency-resilience margin, where all institutions remain solvent with respect to the external sector. We show that this margin is computed exactly by a finite family of linear programs, one per vertex of the uncertainty ball, whereas a single linear program based on the componentwise worst deterioration of external resources yields only a certified lower bound. We extend this framework beyond that margin in three directions. First, we derive an exact mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation for the maximal clearing vector under arbitrary signed external net positions, providing a clearing oracle for robust stress testing when insolvency can occur. Second, we develop certified bounds on the worst-case loss beyond the margin, including insolvency-pattern enumeration, scenario lower bounds, fixed-pattern dual upper bounds, localized certificates, and a regime-generation procedure with monotone gap certificates. Third, we analyze the worst-case loss curve as a function of the perturbation radius. For $\ell_1$ and $\ell_\infty$ price-perturbation sets, the curve is convex, nondecreasing and piecewise linear up to the margin, with breakpoints generated by switches in worst-case shock directions, LP bases, and bank-level activity patterns. Beyond the margin, it remains nondecreasing and piecewise affine, but convexity may fail, the curve may jump upward, and the worst case need not be attained. The framework provides a certifiable MILP/LP methodology for parametric stress testing and interpretable diagnostics identifying the banks responsible for changes in systemic loss.

papers.title: Objective Diversification of Dynamic Hedging
papers.summary: A hedging objective reflects the risk preference of the hedger, so the conventional approach is to estimate the hedge ratio directly under the chosen objective. This paper asks whether that estimate should be used alone. We construct five objective-specific rolling hedge-ratio estimators---minimum variance, least absolute deviation (LAD), downside semivariance, lower-tail quantile, and Expected Shortfall (ES)---from the same historical stock--market returns, and combine the resulting estimates under a fixed final evaluation objective. Separate multi-output ExtraTrees models predict the within-stock-date ranks of the five candidates under MSE, LAD, downside semivariance, and 10\% quantile loss. The design uses pre-specified 60-, 90-, 120-, and 180-day windows with objective-matched rolling estimators as benchmarks. Adaptive weighting improves the corresponding loss in all sixteen objective--window comparisons. Equal weighting, which uses the same objective-specific hedge ratios without state variables or learned reweighting, already improves downside and quantile hedging. The results therefore suggest that estimates generated under other objectives can be useful even when the final hedging preference and evaluation objective are fixed, while adaptive weighting can provide a further improvement.

papers.title: Joint modelling of financial cost and carbon footprint in motor insurance claims: a BINAR(1) decision framework for circular auto parts adoption
papers.summary: Motor insurance claims management increasingly faces a dual objective: controlling claim costs while reducing greenhouse-gas emissions associated with vehicle repair decisions. This paper proposes a bivariate, discrete-time modelling framework that links the dynamics of financial claims and repair-related carbon footprint inspired by a BINAR(1) dependence structure, allowing for temporal persistence, cross-dependence and a positive/negative correlation between the two dimensions. Using externally sourced emission factors and cost information for replacement parts, we operationalise the carbon footprint of claims under two repair pathways: new parts versus circular-economy reused parts (PIEC). We then conduct scenario analyses in which the acceptance rate of reused parts varies, and we quantify the joint implications for expected monetary outlays and CO 2 -equivalent emissions. Results show that higher PIEC acceptance can simultaneously reduce expected emissions and average claim cost, and the magnitude of the joint benefit depends on the dependence structure and persistence captured by the BINAR(1) process. The proposed framework provides a transparent, reproducible tool for insurers to evaluate repair-policy levers and to align claims operations with decarbonisation targets while retaining an explicit stochastic risk perspective.

papers.title: Portfolio-aware scenario transfer of reserve movements: evidence from Lloyd's syndicates
papers.summary: A claims-development movement on one portfolio may not transfer directly as a stress to another size. We estimate how to transfer such scenarios between portfolio sizes, using 632 syndicate-years from 117 Lloyd's syndicates over 2015-2024. The measured movement is the change in gross claims estimates on selected older underwriting cohorts, divided by opening gross claims outstanding plus reserves taken on in the year whose development it includes; it is not a pure measure of opening-reserve deterioration. Its dispersion falls materially with reserve size, and a size-based scale predicts held-out syndicates far better than a single market scale. But the transferred upper tail understates the smallest books: in the smallest reserve-size quartile, six of 158 held-out observations exceeded the transferred 99.5th percentile, against 0.79 expected, from three syndicates. Square-root scaling has descriptively lower held-out pinball loss at 99% and 99.5%, though more misses among the largest books. For a GBP 500m portfolio the transferred empirical 99.5th percentile is 0.34 of reserves (95% credible interval, conditional on the fitted model, 0.23-0.52), against 0.67 in the raw market pool. Both are Syndicate 5820's 2016 movement. The contribution is inspectable scenario comparability, not a calibrated capital quantile or a next-year forecast.
papers.comment: 29 pages, 5 figures, 16 tables. The online supplement (52 pages) and an interactive transfer tool (a self-contained HTML file) are in the ancillary files

papers.title: Credibility Clustering for Experience Rating: An Automated Approach to Risk Group Allocation in Group Life Insurance
papers.summary: In insurance, experience rating plays a crucial role in mitigating adverse selection by adjusting premiums according to historical claims experience. A key step in this process is the classification of insured collectives into homogeneous risk groups. Within group life insurance, this classification traditionally relies on manual decisions and arbitrary thresholds, which may lead to inefficiencies and inconsistent outcomes. This paper proposes a data-driven methodology for automating risk group allocation based on a combination of the multidimensional Bühlmann-Straub model and k-means clustering -- referred to as credibility clustering. By incorporating credibility weights, the method accounts for the varying statistical significance of experience data and ensuresthat risk classifications are both actuarially sound and practically implementable. Empirical results based on real-world group life insurance data from a major European insurer demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms the two k-means benchmark variants considered in the empirical application in terms of viability, temporal stability and accounting for statistical reliability.

papers.title: Exponential Seniority Weighting Chain-Ladder Reserving
papers.summary: We develop a tractable state-space version of the chain-ladder model. The state-space dynamics acts on the accident year axis which, in contrast to the classical chain-ladder model, makes accident years dependent. This state-space version yields an exponential seniority weighting in the chain-ladder factor estimation, and it admits an analytical likelihood representation that enables us to compute the seniority weighted chain-ladder reserves and their prediction uncertainty: the one-year uncertainty is available in closed form and the total uncertainty requires a Monte Carlo simulation from the fully tractable likelihood representation.

papers.title: Robust distortion riskmetrics over Bregman--Wasserstein balls and their intersections
papers.summary: We study the worst-case values of distortion riskmetrics over Bregman--Wasserstein balls around a reference distribution. Unlike the squared $2$-Wasserstein distance, Bregman--Wasserstein divergences can penalize upward and downward deviations differently. Our main result applies to generalized distortion functions $g:[0,1]\to\R$ of bounded variation, with $g(0)=0$ and suitable endpoint regularity, which need not be monotone, normalized, or upper semicontinuous. For strictly convex generators satisfying a two-sided $p$-growth condition, we obtain a one-dimensional dual representation of the worst-case value. When a positive Lagrange multiplier makes the divergence constraint binding, we identify a unique quantile function through a least concave majorant and characterize when it attains the supremum. For absolutely continuous generalized distortion functions, we characterize the solution through an isotonic projection; we also study more general generators and shape constraints, including unimodality. Finally, we extend the analysis to intersections of Bregman--Wasserstein balls, describing models acceptable to several parties involved in decision making, and illustrate the results numerically.

papers.title: Interpretable Allocation and Model-Predictive Rebalancing of Equity Portfolios, Tested on Real and Synthetic Markets
papers.summary: A live equity portfolio poses three problems: which stocks to hold, when to trade, and whether the strategy holds up beyond the observed market. We built one system for all three and tested it on 373 US equities, calibrated on 2014-2024 and traded from January 2025 to September 2026. A selection rule chose stocks by score, by a bandit, or at random, and one of seven weighting rules, four consumer-theory utilities, and three standard portfolios, set share counts under limits on budget, single-stock weight, portfolio volatility, and turnover, with each stock's preference weight a bounded score of its trend, market beta, and the market's recent direction. A model-predictive controller forecasts portfolio value with a multi-asset geometric Brownian motion and re-planned at its horizon, when the value left its forecast band, or at a drawdown stop. To probe deeper declines than the real window held, we also ran the system on simulated markets from per-asset hidden Markov generators with jumps, linked by market and sector factors. On real prices, the stocks chosen mattered more to terminal wealth than the weighting rule, and the early re-plans shrank the worst drawdown in most rule combinations against a fixed calendar without consistently raising wealth. In the deepest simulated declines, every combination, random picks included, ended above simulated SPY and the equal-weight universe in the median, even without early re-plans, so the margin came from shared parts of the system, not from stock selection or re-plan timing. A market hedge that tightened a beta cap as the market weakened cost wealth on real prices but paid off in the most sustained simulated declines, and the generator's persistent trends favored score-based selection more than the real market did, which suggests a synthetic test judges stock selection fairly only if its generator does not build in that persistence.

papers.title: The Laplace transform of the time of ruin in the Cramér--Lundberg model with Erlang $E_2(μ)$ claims: spectrum, exact moments and matrix reduction
papers.summary: We study the Laplace transform of the time of ruin in the classical Cramér--Lundberg model with claims having an Erlang distribution of shape parameter 2. We derive an integro-differential equation with two boundary conditions. For every positive discount rate, we show that its characteristic polynomial has one negative root and two distinct positive roots. Boundedness excludes the growing exponential term and yields a representation of the transform as a sum of two decaying exponentials. We construct a finite-dimensional matrix reduction of the convolution chain. For a model parameter set, we obtain exact expressions for the ruin probability, the mean time of ruin, and higher moments, including the third moment at zero initial surplus. We prove analyticity in the discount rate and justify the resulting moment series. We consider the analytic continuation of the representation to negative discount rates separately. For Erlang claims with an arbitrary positive integer shape parameter, we establish a closed linear system and the asymptotics of the root continuing the zero root at zero discount.

papers.title: RiskReason: A Benchmark for Verifiable Financial Risk Reasoning
papers.summary: Robust financial-risk inference requires more than mathematical correctness. Models must accurately apply conditional rules, maintain evolving financial states, and make decisions that respect operational constraints. This work introduces RiskReason, a benchmark for verifiable financial-risk reasoning that spans diverse risk-management mechanisms. The benchmark includes Standard tasks, which assess individual financial mechanisms, and Long-horizon tasks, which combine multiple mechanisms through extended dependencies. Each task provides reference outcomes, formal specifications, reasoning annotations, and dependency representations to support systematic analysis of model performance. Eleven model configurations are evaluated using strict single-attempt accuracy, complemented by structural and qualitative failure analyses. The strongest configurations achieve 80.0--90.2\% overall accuracy, with several maintaining high performance on composed financial scenarios. However, analysis of failures reveals incorrect risk decisions despite accurate intermediate calculations, inconsistent propagation of financial states, and remediation actions that violate binding constraints. In contrast, some strict evaluation failures result from incomplete reporting rather than incorrect financial conclusions. These findings indicate that aggregate accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize financial-risk reasoning reliability and motivate evaluations that distinguish numerical correctness, state consistency, constraint satisfaction, and decision validity.
papers.comment: 15 pages, Accepted at the Workshop on The 3rd Workshop on LLMs and Generative AI for Finance

papers.title: Robust distortion riskmetrics under symmetry, unimodality, and Wasserstein constraints
papers.summary: We study worst-case distortion riskmetrics over symmetric distributions with prescribed mean and variance in a Wasserstein ball around a reference distribution. Our key contribution is the construction of a reference-dependent auxiliary distortion that encodes the Wasserstein constraint while preserving symmetry under the concave-envelope operation. Under suitable regularity and nondegeneracy conditions, this construction yields sharp upper bounds for distortions of bounded variation, allowing nonmonotonicity and interior discontinuities, and identifies extremal distributions when the bounds are attained. An approximation preserving symmetry and the prescribed moments exactly shows that upper semicontinuous relaxation of the symmetrized distortion leaves the supremum unchanged for budgets strictly above the feasibility threshold. With additional unimodality, symmetry fixes the quantile's concavity-convexity transition at the midpoint, yielding a characterization via $L^2$-projection onto a fixed closed convex cone for absolutely continuous distortions with square-integrable derivatives. Numerical examples for ES, RVaR, and VaR illustrate how shape restrictions and the reference distribution affect feasibility and worst-case risk. Simulations with data-dependent Wasserstein radii examine worst-case ES and feasibility under correctly specified and misspecified shape restrictions.

papers.title: Quantifying Repair Risk in Crypto Option Surfaces
papers.summary: Option desks adjust crypto option quotes into price surfaces that remain within bid-ask intervals and satisfy standard no-arbitrage restrictions across strikes before computing Greeks, hedge quantities, or risk measures. For the same quote panel, however, these constraints may admit multiple such surfaces, which we call admissible repairs, with different downstream outputs. We define the resulting variation as repair risk and propose repair-risk validation, a matched framework for quantifying dispersion in Greeks, hedge quantities, and risk measures. The mechanism is finite-difference amplification: two admissible repairs within price distance $\varepsilon$ can differ in local normalized-strike curvature by $4\varepsilon/h^2$, where $h$ is local normalized-strike spacing. We evaluate repair risk on Deribit BTC and ETH option chains, using $L_1$ and $L_2$ projections of midpoint prices onto the same admissible set as matched controls. Across 108 matched evaluations spanning 18 sampled calendar months, the median 90th percentile of the scaled spot-gamma gap for $L_2$ versus the $ρ=10$ smoothness-penalized repair is nearly twenty times the matched $L_1$--$L_2$ control. We also instantiate NN-Proj, a neural-projection repair, to test whether learned repairs exhibit repair risk. Despite good held-out fit, its downstream outputs remain distinct from those of classical repairs. Across five seeds with the same training window and architecture, its curvature dispersion exceeds the matched $L_1$--$L_2$ control in 17 of 18 months ($p=1.45\times10^{-4}$). For a USD 1 million risk reversal, switching from $L_2$ to the $ρ=10$ repair shifts the median 90th-percentile hedge notional by 18.62 basis points of gross spot notional. VaR-style estimates also exhibit greater dispersion across repairs. The repair rule is therefore part of the risk model, not merely a feasibility check.
papers.comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. Accepted for oral presentation at ACM ICAIF 2026. Contributions: quantifies uncertainty from choosing among admissible option price curves, provides approaches for identifying option chains with potentially large curvature differences, and evaluates the effects on Greeks, hedges, and risk estimates using Deribit BTC and ETH option data

papers.title: Approximate clearing in financial networks with credit default swaps: hardness thresholds, a box algorithm, barriers, and exact solvency at bounded degree
papers.summary: We study approximate clearing in financial networks with credit default swaps. For weak notions (W) and (I), we prove PPAD-hardness below a threshold approximately $0.2530$ and give a polynomial-time interval algorithm above a threshold approximately $0.2834$. On networks whose CDS writers are solvent ex ante, the corresponding bounds are $(13-\sqrt{153})/4$ and $3-2\sqrt{2}$, approximately $0.1577$ and $0.1716$. The thresholds are sharp for bounded-radius algorithms: for (I) on writer-solvent networks, and for (I) and (W) in general. On non-degenerate networks, (W) and (I) have identical hardness and tractability threshold endpoints. For exact-solvency notion (D), PPAD-hardness holds at every rational error $\varepsilon<1$ on non-degenerate networks. On a restricted unit-notional class, let $d$ be the maximum number of CDS contracts held by a core bank, counted with multiplicity. For rational $\varepsilon\in[1/2,1)$, writing $ρ=(1+\varepsilon)/(1-\varepsilon)$, the problem is polynomial-time solvable when $d<(\lceilρ\rceil+1)ρ$ and PPAD-complete otherwise. At $\varepsilon=1/3$ the boundary is $d=5$ versus $d=6$; below $\varepsilon=1/9$, degree $2$ is already PPAD-complete, while degree $1$ is exactly solvable. These degree results concern (D) and do not close the (W)/(I) approximation windows. We also establish a barrier to Pure-Circuit reductions certified by interval propagation under stated interface and auxiliary-bank restrictions. A finite-precision interval algorithm reduces writer-solvent (I) to point selection in near-stalled boxes; selection is polynomial-time when the residual matrix is symmetric or monotone on each strongly connected component. The general and writer-solvent approximation windows remain open.
papers.comment: 119 pages including references and complete proof appendices. Scientific code and supporting materials: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23834656

papers.title: When is the deepest drawdown also the longest?
papers.summary: Does the deepest drawdown take the longest to recover? For random walks with iid increments of positive finite mean, we find that the deepest and longest episodes are eventually distinct almost surely under light-tailed losses, but coincide with probability tending to one under heavy-tailed losses. More precisely, when losses have a finite exponential moment, the deepest episode's duration, relative to the longest among $n$ episodes, converges in probability to an explicit $ρ\in(0,1)$, while its descending duration rank is $n^{1-ρ+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)}$. These limits hold for every fixed number of leading depths; in the Gaussian model, $ρ=1/2$, independently of drift and variance. The separation reflects the different exponential costs of reaching a large depth and sustaining a long episode. For regularly varying losses, a common large loss governs both depth and duration: the duration ratio tends to one almost surely, and for every fixed $k$, the $k$ deepest and $k$ longest episodes have the same indices in the same order with probability tending to one. For any $k_n\to\infty$ with $k_n=o(n)$, the proportion of common episodes among the $k_n$ deepest and $k_n$ longest converges in probability to zero in the light-tailed case and to one in the heavy-tailed case. These ranking laws also hold for completed drawdowns within a deterministic observation horizon.

papers.title: Expected shortfall estimation and capital coverage under overlapping scenarios
papers.summary: Expected shortfall (ES) is routinely estimated from a short sample of profit-and-loss (P&L) scenarios built from overlapping multi-day returns, while the non-parametric estimators applied to such data are designed under independent sampling. We study how this mismatch affects estimation accuracy and capital coverage, and how it interacts with serial dependence and heavy tails in the underlying P&L. Working within the coherent risk estimation framework, we compare six order-statistic-based ES estimators on fit, bias, and capital-coverage metrics. Following the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB), we use a one-year estimation window and ES at the $2.5\%$ confidence level as a benchmark setup. We combine simulations with market data on twelve risk factors and ninety-nine equity portfolios. We show that overlapping sampling does not merely add noise but shifts ES estimates systematically downward, thereby weakening capital coverage. Serial dependence acts in the same direction, and heavy tails amplify both effects. More conservative weighting mitigates the underestimation but does not remove it. On market data, the confidence level at which the estimated capital covers realized losses roughly doubles in median under overlapping sampling for every estimator, while the $\textrm{ES}_{2.5\%}$-to-$\textrm{VaR}_{1\%}$ ratio, which links the FRTB base market risk capital metric to its pre-FRTB predecessor, changes comparatively little. Overlapping sampling can thus substantially understate ES-based capital. Since many banks apply a small set of standard estimators in their FRTB regulatory or economic capital model in a historical simulation approach, this understatement is likely to be common for many institutions, and combining simulation-based assessment of estimation risk with coverage-based diagnostics offers a practical method to detect it in model validation and monitoring.

papers.title: Information Flow and Market Risk: Transformer-Based Evidence on Sentiment and Volatility Dynamics
papers.summary: This study examines whether transformer-based financial news sentiment improves equity volatility forecasts beyond conventional market-based predictors. Using data for eleven US stocks, we compare volatility persistence models with specifications incorporating the VIX, AAII investor sentiment, and news sentiment extracted using ModernFinBERT. The forecasting target is annualized volatility constructed from future averages of trailing 252-session Yang-Zhang estimates, evaluated at horizons of 1, 5, and 22 trading days. Models are assessed through walk-forward testing with expanding and rolling estimation windows, fixed initial hyperparameter selection, and statistical comparisons accounting for multiple testing and serial dependence. Results show that a naive persistence benchmark achieves the lowest average QLIKE loss at all horizons. Although HAR-VIX produces the largest number of individual forecasting wins under expanding windows, it does not achieve the lowest mean loss. Adding text-based sentiment improves HAR forecasts in only two of 33 expanding-window comparisons, and neither improvement remains statistically significant under longer HAC bandwidths. A blinded audit of 2,700 news texts further characterizes the agreement and confidence patterns of ModernFinBERT classifications. The findings do not establish a general incremental forecasting advantage from transformer-based news sentiment. They highlight the importance of strong benchmarks, temporal alignment, robust inference, and careful evaluation of text-derived predictors.

papers.title: CADENCE: Distributional Next-Transaction Forecasting for Business Cash-Flow Underwriting
papers.summary: Recurring cash flows are the backbone of cash-flow underwriting: they separate durable revenue from one-off deposits, expose standing obligations, and ultimately determine ability to pay. For small businesses, recurrence is both indispensable and hard to estimate, because much of their income arrives as ambiguous transfers, most payment streams are short, and schedules follow calendar conventions that frequency-domain methods treat as noise. We present CADENCE, Calendar-Aware Distributional Event Network for Cash-Flow Estimation, a compact causal Transformer that treats each transaction as a token and predicts the amount and a full, nonparametric timing distribution of every cash flow's next payment. Inheriting transaction semantics from an external labeler and a frozen text encoder keeps CADENCE compact yet general across the long tail of small-business counterparties, while predicting a calibrated distribution rather than an opaque embedding makes its outputs interpretable enough to feed existing underwriting models and power credit decisions. Ablations confirm the role of each design choice, with counterparty semantics driving recall on short histories, calendar inputs driving timing accuracy, and no-event supervision driving precision. Against the production FFT baseline, CADENCE improves one-day timing accuracy by 93.3% and next-event F1 by 6.7%, while producing calibrated distributions that serve directly as a confidence gate for downstream decisions. In an end-to-end credit evaluation on production applications, replacing FFT recurrence features with CADENCE features raises KS by 4.8%, raises the approval rate at a fixed loss rate by 18.2%, and lowers the loss rate at a fixed approval rate by 13.1%.

papers.title: An Application of Geometric Riemannian Pricing Algorithm for Valuing Catastrophe Bonds in Incomplete Markets: Market-Consistent Financial Entropy and the Split of Frequency and Severity Risk Premia
papers.summary: This paper presents a framework for pricing catastrophe (CAT) bonds in incomplete markets through Riemannian geometric optimization of financial entropy. We formulate pricing-measure selection as a maximum financial entropy problem on a finite-dimensional manifold of equivalent measures, parameterized by the non-hedgeable market prices of catastrophe frequency and severity risk, with discounting fixed by the default-free term structure. Since unconstrained entropy maximization recovers the physical measure, we incorporate observed secondary-market spreads, both pooled and date by date. For a compound Poisson-generalized Pareto loss model with Wang distortion, we derive closed-form expressions for financial entropy and the Riemannian metric. We show that CAT bond prices depend on frequency and severity premia primarily through the risk-neutral trigger intensity, making the two premia unidentifiable from market data alone; the entropy criterion resolves this ambiguity. Using a hypothetical earthquake CAT bond calibrated to quarterly spreads of Golden State Re II Ltd. (Series 2014-1), we obtain risk-neutral trigger intensities of 6.58 to 10.45 times the physical intensity (9.20 pooled and 18.26 at the end of 2015). The model-implied risk multiple aligns with the market spread-to-expected-loss ratio (8.87 versus 8.81 at issuance). The minimal-entropy measure attributes 53.5% to 63.7% of the log risk multiple to frequency risk, reflecting the selection principle rather than market identification. Finally, equating the coupon with the quoted spread understates the risk multiple by approximately half.

papers.title: Risk measures for infinite-server queues driven by a Cox-BESQ process
papers.summary: This paper introduces a model for infinite-server queues driven by a Cox process with stochastic intensity given by a squared Bessel (BESQ) process. Exploiting the affine structure of the underlying dynamics, we derive a closed-form expression for the joint moment-generating function (MGF) of the arrival intensity, the number of customers in the system, and the integral of the number of customers in the system over a time interval. This MGF can also be obtained at two (or more) dates, thereby allowing an analysis of the time evolution of infinite-server queues driven by a Cox--BESQ process. The availability of these explicit MGFs enables the development of risk measures for these variables, such as the joint moments of the arrival intensity, the number of customers in the system, and the integral of the number of customers in the system over a time interval, conditional on one of these variables exceeding a critical threshold. These risk measures can be determined at one or two dates. They rely essentially on the explicit form of the MGF of the state variables and on Fourier representations of the risk measures. Numerical experiments demonstrate the practical implementation of the proposed methodology and highlight the relevance of the theoretical results.

papers.title: Decorrelating the Advice Layer: A Calibrated Fragility Metric and Tested Mitigations for Synchronized Liquidation in Agentic Wealth Management
papers.summary: Conversational AI agents are turning wealth management into a continuous loop of market analysis, allocation, risk checks and execution, run for millions of clients on a handful of foundation models. We build a multi-asset agent-based model of this layer, calibrated to measured model concentration, cross-model correlation, retail turnover and 33 years of real equity returns, and ask when the layer amplifies market declines and what prevents it. The effective number of independent decision-makers is bounded however many clients the layer serves: about 2.0 at today's consumer concentration. This monoculture of views drives crowding in individual securities and sets the blast radius of a compromised model provider, but it does not drive market-wide liquidation. Index tail losses rise with the square root of agentic adoption, are 1.47-1.90 times larger under an agentic than under a periodic robo-advice architecture, and do not rise with model concentration; synchronized automation (risk overlays, drawdown cuts and attention-driven execution) drives them. A fragility index computed from aggregate flow, public returns and an impact estimate forecasts tail liquidation out of sample (hold-out R^2 of 0.56) far better than concentration or correlation measures. Decorrelating the automation, not the models, works: dispersing overlay parameters, staging execution and a participation breaker together cut tail liquidation by 63% at no measurable cost to client welfare, whereas provider diversification has no effect. Because the statistics required are sums, they can be computed across platforms under secure aggregation with differential privacy at negligible cost for realistic client populations. In historical replays, an agentic layer holding 10% of the market would have deepened the 2020 crash by about 858 basis points.

papers.title: Optimal portfolio choice under green transition timing risk
papers.summary: We study an investor's optimal portfolio choice problem when they account for the impact of a possible future green transition, whose timing is uncertain. We model the green transition as a discontinuity in the stock price processes, driven by a single jump process with constant intensity, in which 'green' stocks increase in value and 'brown' stocks decrease in value. The investor is ambiguous about the timing of the green transition and designs an investment strategy which is robust to this risk. The investor has constant relative risk aversion preferences over both wealth and model ambiguity, which introduce a multiplicative ambiguity penalty for power utility and an additive ambiguity penalty for log utility. We separate the problem into pre- and post-transition cases, derive the solution, and provide a verification theorem. We further show that the log utility, ambiguity-neutral, and worst-case problems are obtained as special cases of our general problem. In a case study with one green and one brown stock, we show that when the stock prices are positively correlated, an investor who is aware of transition risk increases their investment in the green stock and reduces their investment in the brown stock, compared to when they ignore the possibility of a transition. We illustrate the difference between an ambiguity-averse and a risk-averse investor, and show how an ambiguity-averse investor re-allocates their portfolio as their view on the probability of a green transition changes.

papers.title: Optimal collective investment under regulatory uncertainty
papers.summary: We study optimal collective investment subject to a Value-at-Risk (VaR)-type constraint that accounts for uncertainty about future regulatory requirements. The constraint incorporates several possible wealth thresholds and imposes a minimum weighted average probability of meeting them. We characterize the optimal terminal wealth, which combines regions of constant wealth at regulatory thresholds with Merton-type investment regions. Unlike a classical VaR constraint with only one threshold, our formulation generates protection against several thresholds. For two possible thresholds, we identify when both are protected and when protection concentrates on the larger one. Numerical results show that the regulatory constraint can substantially reshape the optimal payoff and generate large welfare losses relative to unconstrained investment when the required compliance probability is high, even the smaller wealth threshold is high, or initial capital is limited. In heterogeneous investor pools, welfare losses depend strongly on the composition of the risk aversions and the Pareto weights governing risk sharing. Losses are particularly pronounced when highly risk-averse investors dominate the pool. Moreover, investors with smaller capital contributions can bear disproportionately large shares of the total welfare loss, while larger contributors may bear less than their capital-proportional share. Thus, regulatory uncertainty not only reduces aggregate welfare but can also create substantial disparities in how its costs are distributed among investors.
